articles.title: Indefiniteness: Claiming a Measurement Without the Test Method
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC (Fed. Cir. 2026)
We talked about this particular issue in my patent law class today - the same day the Federal Circuit released its decision, although I had not read the case yet at that time. There are a surprising number of cases that turn on a measurement that is claimed without any indication in the claim or specification indicating how to actually make that measurement. Or, as in this case provide multiple methods of measurement that each would result in different claim scope.
Cocona's US8945287 covers a waterproof breathable membrane and each asserted claim requires a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) "from about 600 g/m2/day to about 11000 g/m2/day." The claims do not say how MVTR is to be measured.
The problem though is that the specification describes more than one test, including an upright cup method and an inverted cup method, and the two can give very different numbers. Test data in Cocona's own provisional application showed a sample at 223 under the upright cup and 1,394 under the inverted cup - outside the claimed range under one test and inside it under the other. The district court found the claims indefinite. On appeal, the Federal Circuit has affirmed -- holding that the patent gave no guidance on which of its methods to use and so a skilled artisan could not determine the scope of the claims with reasonable certainty.

articles.title: Rule 60(d) Independent Actions and the Conversion of Merits Into Jurisdiction
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Traxcell lost its 2017 patent suit against Verizon in the Eastern District of Texas, and then lost the fee fight that followed. The district court awarded Verizon attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 -- roughly half a million dollars -- and the Federal Circuit affirmed. Traxcell - represented by Bill Ramey - then filed a new lawsuit in the Western District of Texas, an independent action under Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(d)(1), asking Judge Albright to declare the fee award void. Traxcell's theory: the Federal Circuit's merits mandate in the first appeal stripped the Eastern District of power to award fees afterward. Judge Albright rejected that theory on the merits. Ramey appealed, but rather than deciding that question, the Federal Circuit vacated and ordered dismissal -- holding that the Western District never had jurisdiction over the case.
The opinion makes two jurisdictional rulings about the same lawsuit.
I question the first holding. As I explain below, Traxcell's challenge was about the impact of an appellate mandate on a lower court's jurisdiction, and did not directly raise any patent law issue.
And, IMO, the second holding is also wrong, at least in part, because it treats Traxcell's failure to meet the Beggerly standard for an independent action as a lack of jurisdiction - converting the merits into jurisdiction.
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

Traxcell Technologies, LLC v. Cellco Partnership, No. 25-1496, --- F.4th --- (Fed. Cir. Nov. 16, 2026)

Traxcell lost its 2017 patent suit against Verizon in the Eastern District of Texas, and then lost the fee fight that followed. The district court awarded Verizon attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 -- roughly half a million dollars -- and the Federal Circuit affirmed. Traxcell - represented by Bill Ramey - then filed a new lawsuit in the Western District of Texas, an independent action under Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(d)(1), asking Judge Albright to declare the fee award void. Traxcell's theory: the Federal Circuit's merits mandate in the first appeal stripped the Eastern District of power to award fees afterward. Judge Albright rejected that theory on the merits. Ramey appealed, but rather than deciding that question, the Federal Circuit vacated and ordered dismissal -- holding that the Western District never had jurisdiction over the case.

The opinion makes two jurisdictional rulings about the same lawsuit.

  1. The court concluded this case arose under the patent laws because it was a collateral attack on a § 285 award. As a patent case, the appeal was properly before the Federal Circuit.
  2. The court held that the district court lacked jurisdiction over the collateral action because the allegations fell far short of the "grave miscarriage of justice" standard for collateral attack. United States v. Beggerly, 524 U.S. 38 (1998). In addition, the appellate panel concluded that one district court cannot entertain an independent action to undo another district's judgment after it has been affirmed on appeal.

I question the first holding. As I explain below, Traxcell's challenge was about the impact of an appellate mandate on a lower court's jurisdiction, and did not directly raise any patent law issue.

And, IMO, the second holding is also wrong, at least in part, because it treats Traxcell's failure to meet the Beggerly standard for an independent action as a lack of jurisdiction - converting the merits into jurisdiction.

articles.title: Federal Circuit Reversal Rates by Tribunal: District Courts vs. the PTAB
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch

Since 2021, the Federal Circuit changed the judgment (reversed or vacated, in whole or in part) in 33% of district court patent decisions, but in only 19% of PTAB trial decisions. But, back in 2021, the two rates were almost identical. The gap opened in 2022 and has persisted, even after accounting for year, which side appealed, and the issues on appeal.

articles.title: 18 Years of Federal Circuit Mandamus: The Rise and Fall of the Texas Venue Surge
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
In early October, 2026, the Federal Circuit granted Google's mandamus petition and ordered USC v. Google transferred from Judge Albright's (former) Austin docket to the Northern District of California. This was the court's first mandamus grant since In re Honeywell in January 2024. The court had denied the prior 100+ mandamus petitions. The recent drought followed much more actions by the court in 2021 and 2022.
Every mandamus grant since 2019 (45 total) came from a Texas district court case, seeking a venue ruling. For Texas venue petitions filed 2021 through 2023, the court granted about 44%. Since then it has granted only 4%: one petition, Google's. And now, with Judge Albright off the bench, everyone has calmed down a bit.
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

In re Google LLC, No. 2026-157 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 6, 2026) (nonprecedential order)

In early October, 2026, the Federal Circuit granted Google's mandamus petition and ordered USC v. Google transferred from Judge Albright's (former) Austin docket to the Northern District of California. This was the court's first mandamus grant since In re Honeywell in January 2024. The court had denied the prior 100+ mandamus petitions.  The recent drought followed much more actions by the court in 2021 and 2022.

Every mandamus grant since 2019 (45 total) came from a Texas district court case, seeking a venue ruling. For Texas venue petitions filed 2021 through 2023, the court granted about 44%. Since then it has granted only 4%: one petition, Google's. And now, with Judge Albright off the bench, everyone has calmed down a bit.

articles.title: The Director Returns IPR Merits to the PTAB
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
This is a follow-up to my September post on Professor John Duffy's move to the USPTO. Duffy was sworn in as General Counsel on October 5, and the Office has now expanded his title to General Counsel and Supervisory Solicitor. Joining him as Deputy General Counsel and Solicitor is Professor Greg Dolin (Baltimore). Dolin is a former clerk for Judge Pauline Newman and later represented her in her lawsuit against Chief Judge Moore and the Federal Circuit's Judicial Council.
Duffy and Dolin are law professors and creative appellate litigators. I expect to see some interesting developments.
Duffy's first visible work product was announced on November 10, 2026. In a memorandum co-signed with Director Squires, the Office is returning the merits portion of IPR and PGR institution decisions to the PTAB, effective November 16.
The Director will keep the initial screen on discretionary and other non-merits factors. Petitions that survive go to a three-judge panel that decides institution on the merits on the Director's behalf -- and if that panel institutes, a different panel will conduct the trial. The memo also tightens the merits standard. A petition fails if it falls short on a substantial majority of the challenged claims, and a claim whose arguments are in "equipoise" counts against the petitioner. Tie goes to denial.
